quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

## Review of pe_005 (a_013 → Patrick Flynn / I1)

### What the link says

pe_005 connects assertion **a_013** — extracted from the 1908 Schuylkill County death certificate (role: `deceased`) — to tree person **I1 (Patrick Flynn)** at confidence **`confident`**. The recorded rationale notes matching names, death location consistent with known residence, and that the certificate names Thomas Flynn as father.

---

### Key findings

**The confidence tier is arguably defensible — but the rationale is not adequately supported.** Here's why:

#### What holds up
The identity link (is this the right Patrick Flynn?) is corroborated by two prior census links (pe_001 and pe_004, both `confident`) that place Patrick Flynn in Schuylkill County in 1850 and 1860. A Patrick Flynn dying in the same county in 1908 coheres with that residence chain. On that basis alone, `confident` is a defensible tier.

#### What's wrong with the rationale

1. **Required structural checks are missing.** The rationale omits the mandatory date check (record's age-derived birth year vs. tree person's birth year, with gap in years) and the residence check (record place/year vs. nearest attested residence). These are not optional — they are the backbone of the identity verification.

2. **null match_score is unexplained.** No account is given of whether a `same_person` similarity call was made and returned null, or was never called. For an assertion of this type, the instructions require either the score or an explanation of its absence.

3. **Circular reasoning.** The rationale cites "Names Thomas Flynn as father" as identity corroboration — but that is precisely the claim a_013 *makes*. Using the assertion's own content to confirm it belongs to I1 is circular. The actual identity corroboration comes from the census record chain, which is not mentioned.

4. **Informant unreliability not flagged.** The informant (James Brown, son-in-law, `family_not_present`) gave Pennsylvania as Patrick's birthplace in companion assertion a_012, when census records say Ireland. That known inaccuracy is directly relevant context for a_013 — a hearsay parentage claim from the same informant — and is nowhere acknowledged in pe_005.

---

### Summary verdict

| Aspect | Status |
|---|---|
| Confidence tier (`confident`) | Defensible — supported by the broader census corroboration chain |
| Date check line | **Missing** |
| Residence check line | **Missing** |
| match_score accounting | **Missing** |
| Identity reasoning | **Circular** — relies on the assertion's own content |
| Informant bias disclosure | **Missing** |

The link is probably correct, but the written rationale behind it cannot stand as a reliable audit trail in its current form. A revised rationale should ground the `confident` tier in the census corroboration (not the death certificate alone), add the required check lines, account for the null score, and flag the informant's demonstrated unreliability.

Would you like me to draft a corrected rationale for your review and approval before any change is saved?

I now have everything needed for a complete review. This is review-only mode — no writes will be made.

---

## Review of pe_005 (a_013 → I1, Patrick Flynn)

### What the link says

pe_005 connects assertion a_013 — extracted from the 1908 Schuylkill County death certificate (record `ark:/61903/1:1:MDEF`, role `deceased`) — to tree person I1 (Patrick Flynn) at confidence `confident`. The recorded rationale is: "Death certificate for Patrick Flynn, d. 1908, Schuylkill County. Names match, death location matches known residence. Names Thomas Flynn as father."

---

### What a_013 actually is

This is the first thing to pin down, because it changes the analysis. a_013's `fact_type` is `relationship` ("Father: Thomas Flynn"), not a death or birth fact. It is a secondary-quality assertion — informant James Brown (son-in-law), `informant_proximity: family_not_present` — reporting what he was told about his father-in-law's parentage. The same informant supplied the birth year in a_012, and the extractor's own `informant_bias_notes` on that sister assertion flag him as unreliable: he gave Pennsylvania as birthplace when census records say Ireland.

The **content** of a_013 (Thomas Flynn is Patrick's father) is therefore weak evidence — secondary, hearsay, and from an informant already shown to have given wrong biographical information about Patrick's origins. That matters for the parentage question, but pe_005 is not directly about the parentage claim. pe_005 is about **identity**: is the deceased named in this certificate the same person as tree person I1?

---

### Identity assessment (the correct scope of pe_005)

The identity question — does this death certificate record the death of the tree person Patrick Flynn (I1)? — is answered by the certificate's direct facts (a_011: died 12 March 1908, Schuylkill County, PA), not by a_013 alone. The relevant corroborating context from the broader record set:

- pe_001 and pe_004 (both `confident`) already link I1 to the 1850 and 1860 Schuylkill County census enumerations — establishing him as a Patrick Flynn living in that county for decades.
- The death certificate places a Patrick Flynn dying in 1908 in the same county — consistent with the tree person's known residence cluster.
- The tree person's `diedByYear` is 1908, drawn from this very certificate's death fact (a_011).

Across those three records, name, location, and life-span all cohere. On the identity question alone, the `confident` tier is defensible — not because the death certificate stands alone, but because it is consistent with two prior census links.

---

### Problems with the rationale as written

The confidence tier may be salvageable, but the rationale has several significant deficiencies:

**1. Required structural elements are missing.** The instructions mandate two check lines before any tier is chosen:
- "Date check: [record's birth/christening or age-derived year] vs [tree person's birth year]: gap N years." Neither the record nor the tree person gives an unambiguous birth year on a_013 itself (a_013 is a relationship assertion, not a birth fact), but the companion a_012 gives 1845; the tree attests approximately 1845. The required line was simply omitted.
- "Residence check: [record place, year] vs [nearest attested residence, year]: same / neighbouring / outside." Schuylkill County 1908 vs. Schuylkill County from the 1860 census — this is the same county, and the check would be trivially "same." But the line is not present, so a reviewer cannot see that verification was done.

**2. The match_score is null with no explanation.** The instructions require that a null score either be explained (the tool found no reachable persona for this assertion, or the candidate was minted from this persona) or be derived from a `same_person` call. The rationale says nothing about whether `same_person` was called. For a relationship assertion, a separate call is required because it names a second person; if the tool refused or no persona was reachable, that finding belongs in the rationale.

**3. The paternity claim is cited as identity evidence — this is circular.** The rationale says "Names Thomas Flynn as father" as if that corroborates the identity of the deceased as I1. But "Thomas Flynn as father" is precisely what a_013 asserts; using it to confirm that a_013 belongs to I1 is circular. The identity corroboration comes from name, location, and the census record chain — not from the parentage claim this assertion makes.

**4. The birthplace conflict is not acknowledged.** The companion assertion a_012 (from the same record, same informant) gives birthplace as Pennsylvania, while census records say Ireland. The extractor flagged this in the bias notes. Even though this conflict does not undermine the identity of the deceased (a wrong birthplace does not mean a different person died), the unreliability of the informant is relevant context for the rationale on a_013 — particularly given that a_013 is the informant's hearsay report of the paternity, and pe_005 is the link that carries that assertion into the tree. A reviewer reading only pe_005's rationale would not know the informant was demonstrably inaccurate about another biographical detail in the same document.

---

### Summary verdict

The **confidence tier (`confident`) is arguably defensible** for the identity link — the deceased Patrick Flynn in Schuylkill County in 1908 is almost certainly the same man who appears in the 1850 and 1860 census records in that county. But the **rationale as written does not make that case**. It omits the required date and residence check lines, gives no account of the null match_score, leans on the very paternity claim the assertion asserts as if it were identity corroboration, and does not flag the informant's known unreliability.

An improved rationale would: (1) include the date check and residence check lines; (2) state that match_score is null and why; (3) ground the `confident` tier in the two-census corroboration pattern, not in the death certificate alone; (4) note that the secondary informant was already shown to have given wrong birthplace data, which is context for reading a_013's paternity claim.

---

If you would like me to draft the improved rationale text and then ask your authorization before updating pe_005, say the word and I will do that.

---

The death certificate for Patrick Flynn is linked to him in the tree at a "very confident" level, but the explanation recorded for that link has gaps: it is missing the required date and location cross-checks, it does not say whether a formal similarity score was ever calculated, and it quietly uses the very parentage claim the record makes as if it were proof the record belongs to the right Patrick — which is circular reasoning. The informant on this record (a son-in-law) also gave a wrong birthplace in the same document, and that is not mentioned. The link is probably defensible at the same confidence level, but the written reasoning behind it needs to be strengthened before it can stand as a reliable audit trail.
